A B S T R A C T
The reduction of sulfate to sulfide is a critical factor limiting the efficiency of anaerobic digestion in treating 
sulfate-containing organic wastewater. This study proposes a synergistic operational strategy that combines 
nitrate addition and microaeration to inhibit sulfate reduction and enhance anaerobic digestion performance. 
The combined application of nitrate (100–200 mg NO3
−-N/L) and microaeration (Dissolved oxygen: 0.20–0.25 
mg/L) significantly promoted extracellular polymeric substance secretion and facilitated sludge granulation. 
Compared to the control group, which was operated without microaeration or nitrate addition, the combined 
strategy improved chemical oxygen demand removal efficiency and methane production by 48.2–49.8 % and 
138.5–141.5 %, respectively, surpassing the enhancements achieved by nitrate addition alone (28.5–36.0 % and 
69.2–86.2 %) or microaeration alone (38.3 % and 87.7 %, respectively). This synergistic approach inhibited the

elucidate the microbial community dynamics and metabolic pathways driving the enhanced anaerobic digestion 
of sulfate-containing organic wastewater under nitrate and microaeration conditions. This study provides a novel 
and effective strategy for optimizing the anaerobic digestion of sulfate-containing organic wastewater with 
substantial implications for sulfide control in wastewater treatment systems.
1. Introduction
Sulfate-containing organic wastewater (SOW) is generated by 
various industrial sectors, including the petrochemical, pharmaceutical, 
textile dyeing, mining processing, and food processing industries 
(Cetecioglu et al., 2019; Jung et al., 2019; Zak et al., 2021). Directly 
discharging untreated SOW can severely disrupt aquatic ecosystems and 
threaten aquatic organisms and human health. Therefore, the effective 
treatment of SOW is of significant importance for environmental pro­
tection and sustainable development.
Biological treatment methods, particularly anaerobic digestion, are 
widely used to manage organic wastewater because of their operational 
simplicity and cost-effectiveness. Anaerobic digestion offers multiple 
advantages over aerobic treatment technologies, including reduced 
aeration requirements, lower operating costs, a high organic loading 
capacity, minimal sludge production, and generating secondary energy 
in the form of methane (Fang et al., 2019). However, the chemical ox­
ygen demand (COD) removal efficiency in the treatment of SOW 
generally remains below 80 % (Deng et al., 2022; Li et al., 2022), pri­
marily because of the proliferation of sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB). 
These bacteria reduce sulfate to sulfides through dissimilatory sulfate 
reduction, leading to sulfide accumulation, inhibiting microbial activity, 
and reducing the overall efficiency of anaerobic digestion. Free 
hydrogen sulfide (H2S), in particular, is highly toxic and capable of 
penetrating cell membranes, forming cross-links within polypeptide 
chains, altering protein structures, and inhibiting microbial metabolic 
functions (Shi et al., 2024). Previous studies have shown that meth­
anogenic activity is significantly inhibited when free H2S concentrations 
exceed 50 mg/L, resulting in a 50 % reduction in methane production 
(Chen et al., 2008; Gil-Garcia et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020). Further­
more, SRB exhibits a stronger substrate affinity for hydrogen and acetate 
than methanogens, exacerbating competition for these substrates and 
further suppressing methane production (Lu et al., 2016).
Various strategies have been explored to mitigate the adverse effects 
of sulfate on anaerobic digestion, including chemical precipitation and 
iron salt-based methods. Chemical precipitation with barium salts, cal­
cium salts, or ettringite has been used to remove sulfate prior to diges­
tion (Larraguibel et al., 2020; Pratinthong et al., 2021). The use of iron 
salts, such as FeCl2 and zero-valent iron, has been shown to mitigate 
sulfide toxicity by reacting with sulfides to form iron sulfides, thereby 
reducing their harmful effects on microbial communities in anaerobic 
systems (Juntupally et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2019). In particular, the 
precipitation and coagulation processes generate sludge that can be 
potentially toxic due to the accumulation of heavy metals and other 
hazardous substances. Therefore, the safe disposal or treatment of this 
sludge is essential to prevent environmental contamination and sec­
ondary risks (Zhao et al., 2024). In addition, operational adjustments, 
such as maintaining influent pH above 8.0 and optimizing the COD to 
sulfur ratio and implementing two-phase anaerobic digestion, have been 
explored to alleviate sulfide-induced inhibition (Hu et al., 2022b; 
Rajendran et al., 2020; Rodriguez et al., 2012). These interventions fail 
to completely eliminate sulfate reduction, and their effectiveness in 
enhancing anaerobic digestion remains limited. Thus, there is an urgent 
need to develop innovative and cost-effective strategies to mitigate 
sulfate reduction and enhance the anaerobic digestion of SOW.
Nitrate has been widely recognized as an effective inhibitor of sulfate 
reduction in anaerobic systems. Compared to other chemical additives, 
nitrate is not only readily available from industrial sources such as 
petrochemical, steel, and fertilizer production, but is also abundant in 
nitrification effluents from wastewater treatment plants (Abascal et al., 
2022; Inaba et al., 2022). Harnessing wastewater-derived nitrate for 
SOW treatment offers the dual benefits of suppressing sulfide formation 
and implementing a circular “waste-to-treat-waste” strategy. The sup­
pression of SRB by nitrate occurs primarily through competition for 
electron donors by nitrate-reducing bacteria (NRB), as well as the pro­
duction of nitrite during denitrification, which further inhibits SRB ac­
tivity (Lai et al., 2020; Greene et al., 2003; Zhao et al., 2009). 
Additionally, the enrichment of sulfur-oxidizing nitrate-reducing bac­
teria (SoNRB) promotes the oxidation of sulfides to sulfate or elemental 
sulfur, thereby alleviating the inhibitory effects of sulfides on meth­
anogenesis (Cai et al., 2021). Experimental studies have demonstrated 
the effectiveness of nitrate addition in enhancing SOW treatment. For 
example, supplementation with 300 mg/L nitrate-nitrogen decreased 
sulfate removal from 80.5 % to 68.0 % and simultaneously increased 
COD removal from 63.3 % to 83.1 % (Liao et al., 2014). Besides nitrate, 
microaeration has also been shown to inhibit sulfate reduction and 
improve anaerobic digestion performance. Under controlled low-oxygen 
conditions, the activity of sulfide-oxidizing bacteria (SOB) is enhanced, 
facilitating the conversion of sulfide to less harmful sulfur species and 
markedly reducing H2S emissions (Nguyen and Khanal, 2018). For 
instance, Zhou et al. (2007) demonstrated that increasing the air 
sparging rate from 0 to 6 mL/(L⋅min) during anaerobic treatment of pulp 
mill wastewater reduced the sulfide concentration from 400 to 200 
mg/L, while increased COD removal by 40 % and methane production 
by 700 %. Similarly, elevating dissolved oxygen levels from 0.02 to 0.25 
mg/L improved COD removal from 32.5 % to 69.3 % in anaerobic 
digestion systems (Yu et al., 2014). Although previous studies have 
examined the individual effects of nitrate addition and microaeration on 
the anaerobic digestion performance of SOW, most have primarily 
focused on digestion efficiency and microbial community composition. 
There has been limited exploration of the physicochemical characteris­
tics of sludge and the distribution of functional genes under these con­
ditions. However, few studies have systematically investigated the 
synergistic interaction between nitrate addition and microaeration. In 
particular, their combined influence on anaerobic digestion efficiency, 
sulfate reduction, and the associated mechanistic pathways remains 
poorly understood. From an engineering perspective, it is also necessary 
to determine the threshold concentration of nitrate under microaerobic 
conditions at which sulfate reduction begins to be inhibited, as well as to 
evaluate the feasibility of implementing such combined strategies in 
practical wastewater treatment systems.
To address these knowledge gaps, this study systematically investi­
gated the synergistic effects of microaeration and nitrate addition on the 
anaerobic digestion of SOW. The impacts of varying nitrate concentra­
tions under microaerobic conditions on pollutant removal efficiency, 
sludge physicochemical properties, microbial community structure, and 
the abundance of functional genes were comprehensively examined. 
This study not only elucidated the underlying mechanisms by which

2. Materials and methods
2.1. Seed sludge and synthetic SOW
Seed sludge was obtained from a wastewater treatment station at the 
Guangdong University of Petrochemical Technology, China. The volatile 
suspended solid (VSS) to total suspended solid (TSS) ratio was 0.55. The 
synthetic SOW was prepared according to the nutrient composition 
typically found in long-chain dicarboxylic acid (LCDA) wastewater from 
petrochemical industries. Due to its relatively simple composition, with 
glucose (C6H12O6) as the primary carbon source, this approach mini­
mized the potential confounding effects of more complex organic sub­
strates, thereby enabling a more precise assessment of the impacts of the 
experimental variables (nitrate addition and microaeration) on micro­
bial metabolism. The sulfate ions were supplied by sodium sulfate 
(Na2SO4). Ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) and potassium dihydrogen 
phosphate (KH2PO4) were added as nitrogen and phosphorus sources, 
respectively, to achieve a COD:N:P ratio of approximately 200:5:1. Trace 
elements were added according to the protocol described by Chen et al. 
(2017). Sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) was added as a buffering agent at 
concentrations ranging from 840 to 1344 mg/L to maintain the pH of 
wastewater within the range of 8.0–8.5.
2.2. Experimental setup and operation procedure
The experiment was conducted using three UASB reactors equipped 
with an external aeration device (Fig. 1). R1 served as the control group, 
with no nitrate addition or microaeration, for the first 135 days. R2 was 
the experimental group with both microaeration and nitrate addition, 
while R3 served as a control group with only nitrate addition. Each 
UASB reactor had an effective volume of 4.7 L, internal diameter of 74 
mm, and a height of 1195 mm. The synthetic SOW was introduced into 
the UASB reactor via a peristaltic influent pump and transferred to an 
external aeration unit using a second peristaltic pump (recirculating 
pump 1) for aeration. The aerated wastewater was subsequently recir­
culated into the reactor along with the influent using a recirculating 
pump (recirculating pump 2). The gases released during aeration and 
anaerobic digestion were directed through a NaOH absorption bottle, 
which served to remove both H2S and CO2, thereby preventing their 
release into the laboratory environment. For periodic monitoring of 
methane and H2S concentrations, the NaOH absorption bottle was 
temporarily removed, and the biogas was collected directly into gas 
sampling bags for subsequent analysis. In R2, the dissolved oxygen (DO) 
level was controlled by recirculating aerated wastewater from an 
external aeration device. The reflux ratio was maintained at 200 %, 
thereby keeping the DO concentration in the UASB was maintained 
within a range of 0.20–0.25 mg/L. Throughout the experimental period, 
the hydraulic retention time (HRT) was maintained at 24 h, and the 
operational temperature was controlled at 38 ± 1 ◦C using a water bath.
The reactors were operated for 166 d. During the initial 12 d, the 
influent sulfate concentration in all three reactors was maintained at 
400 mg/L, whereas the influent COD gradually increased from 500 to 
1500 mg/L. From day 12 to day 166, the influent COD was set at 1500 
mg/L, achieving a COD/SO4
2−ratio of 3.75 to ensure sufficient carbon 
availability for sulfate reduction (Li et al., 2024a). To evaluate the ef­
fects of nitrate concentration and microaerobic conditions on anaerobic 
digestion for SOW treatment, nitrate was sequentially introduced into 
the influents of reactors R2 and R3 at concentrations of 50, 100, and 200 
mg NO3
−-N/L on days 1, 76, and 113, respectively. These concentrations 
were chosen based on the typical range (50–300 mg NO3
- -N/L) reported 
in the literature to effectively suppress SRB and enhance anaerobic 
digestion (Liao et al., 2014; Cai et al., 2021), as well as the experimental 
goal of identifying the minimum nitrate dosage required to significantly 
improve treatment efficiency. To assess the effect of microaeration alone 
on anaerobic digestion during SOW treatment, aeration was performed 
in the external recirculation device of R1 from day 136 to day 166. 
During this phase, the reflux ratio was maintained at 200 %, and the DO 
concentration in the UASB reactor was controlled within the range of 
0.20–0.25 mg/L, consistent with the operational parameters used for R2.
2.3. Analytical methods
The COD, TSS, VSS, and sludge volume index (SVI30) were analyzed 
using standardized methods (APHA and AWWA, 2005). Nitrate, nitrite 
and sulfate concentrations were determined via ion chromatography 
(Thermo Fisher, ICS-600, USA), whereas sulfide concentrations were 
measured using the methylene blue method (Trüper and Schlegel, 
1964). The pH and DO were measured with a portable pH meter 
(SMART SENSOR, PH 838, China) and a portable dissolved oxygen 
meter (SMART SENSOR, AT9210, China), respectively. The contents of 
methane (CH4) and H2S were determined using gas chromatography 
(Agilent Technologies 6890N, Santa Clara, CA, USA) and a hydrogen 
sulfide detection tube (Gastec, No.4H, China), respectively. The volumes 
of CH4 and H2S were determined using a 100 mL syringe, with the 
measurements recorded at a temperature of 298.15 K and a pressure of 
101.325 kPa. The competitive relationship between SRB and metha­
nogens for substrate utilization was quantitatively evaluated using the 
electron flow ratio of SRB, which was calculated according to Equation

2.4. Microbial community analysis
Sludge samples were collected from the UASB reactors operating 
under varying conditions to analyze the microbial community structure. 
DNA was extracted using the MolPure Soil DNA Kit. The V4 region of the 
16S rRNA gene was amplified with universal primers 515F (5′-GTGY­

Functional gene profiles were predicted from 16S rRNA sequencing 
data using the PICRUSt pipeline, with functional annotation based on 
the latest KEGG database, as detailed by Langille et al. (2013). To

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Reactors performance
The variations in COD removal, sulfate removal, and electron flow 
ratio across different reactors over the experimental period are shown in 
Fig. 2(a–f). In the control group R1, which was operated strictly under 
anaerobic conditions without nitrate addition or microaeration during 
the first 135 days, the average removal efficiencies of COD and sulfate, 
as well as the electron flow ratio, were 47.0 %, 96.7 %, and 39.5 %, 
respectively. This prolonged anaerobic operation ensured that R1 
functioned as a stable control reactor prior to the introduction of 
microaeration. Microaeration was subsequently introduced to R1 on day 
136, after which the effluent COD and sulfate concentrations stabilized 
within approximately 15 days. The rapid stabilization of these perfor­
mance indicators suggests that R1 reached a functional steady state 
under microaeration conditions, enabling a robust evaluation of 
microaeration effects within this operational period. Correspondingly, 
the average COD removal efficiency during the microaeration period 
increased markedly to 85.37 %, whereas the average sulfate removal 
efficiency and electron flow ratio decreased to 33.14 % and 7.57 %, 
respectively. These findings are consistent with those of previous studies 
demonstrating that microaeration enhances COD removal by suppress­
ing the competition between SRB and substrates (Muller et al., 2022; 
Ruan et al., 2019). Reactor R2 was operated with microaeration and 
nitrate addition, whereas reactor R3 was operated with nitrate addition. 
In reactors R2 and R3, the nitrate concentrations were sequentially 
increased to 50, 100, and 200 mg NO3
−-N/L on days 1, 76, and 113, 
respectively, marking the beginning of each operational phase. How­
ever, nitrate in R2 and R3 was completely removed throughout the 
entire experimental period, and no accumulation of nitrite was observed 
(Fig. S1). As the nitrate concentration increased, the COD removal in 
both R2 and R3 improved significantly, whereas the sulfate removal and 
electron flow ratios declined. Under all nitrate concentrations, R2 
demonstrated higher COD removal and lower sulfate removal and 
electron flow ratios than R3. Under typical conditions with nitrate 
concentrations of 100 and 200 mg NO3
−-N/L, the average COD removal 
efficiencies of R2 were 95.2 % and 96.9 %, respectively. These values 
surpassed those of R1 (85.4 %) under microaeration alone between days 
136 and 166, and R3 (83.1 %) at 200 mg NO3
−-N/L from days 113–166. 
Although the COD removal efficiencies of R2 were comparable under 
both 100 and 200 mg NO3
−-N/L conditions, average sulfate removal was 
59.9 % at 100 mg NO3
−-N/L, markedly higher than the 10.8 % observed 
at 200 mg NO3
−-N/L. The increased COD removal in R2 under the 100 
mg NO3
−-N/L condition can be attributed to the synergistic effect of 
microaeration, which promotes the removal of sulfide from the aqueous 
phase and its subsequent oxidation, thereby mitigating sulfide inhibition 
on microbial activity (Nguyen and Khanal, 2018). When the nitrate 
concentration was increased to 200 mg NO3
−-N/L, sulfate reduction was 
further inhibited. In R2, the average sulfate removal and electron flow 
ratio decreased to 10.8 % and 2.3 %, respectively, while R3 exhibited 
corresponding values of 70.9 % and 17.1 %, respectively. These results 
indicate that both nitrate addition and microaeration suppressed sulfate 
reduction to varying extents, with the combined effects of microaeration 
and nitrate addition in R2 producing a more pronounced inhibitory ef­
fect on sulfate reduction. Importantly, nitrate was completely removed 
in both R2 and R3 across all operational phases with influent NO3
−-N 
concentrations ranging from 50 to 200 mg/L (Fig. S1). No residual ni­
trate was detected in the effluent, demonstrating that nitrate supple­
mentation at these levels does not result in nitrate accumulation and is 
unlikely to negatively impact downstream wastewater treatment 
processes.
The variations in the effluent sulfide concentration and H2S pro­
duced across the different reactors are shown in Fig. 2(g). In the control 
reactor R1 (operated without inhibitory conditions during the first 135 
days), the sulfide concentration remained stable at 15.3 mg/L, with 
hydrogen sulfide production averaging 519.1 mg/d. Following 31 days 
of microaeration operation, these values decreased by 81.88 % and 
64.26 %, respectively, reaching 2.8 mg/L and 185.5 mg/d. These results 
indicate that microaeration conditions effectively suppress sulfide for­
mation, which agrees with the results of previous studies (Nguyen and 
Khanal, 2018; Zhou et al., 2007). The effluent pH in both R2 and R3 
exhibited a progressive increase in response to elevated influent nitrate 
concentrations. This effect was particularly pronounced at nitrate dos­
ages exceeding 100 mg NO3
−-N/L, with pH values in R2 and R3 consis­
tently surpassing those observed in R1 (Fig. S2). The increased pH was 
primarily attributable to the alkalinity generation during denitrification 
processes. In reactor R3, the effluent sulfide concentrations exhibited an 
increasing trend with increasing nitrate concentration. A higher pH 
environment facilitated the conversion of H2S to its less toxic ionic form 
(HS−), thereby decreasing the concentration of dissolved H2S and 
mitigating its inhibitory impact on microbial communities. Therefore, 
although the sulfide concentration in R3 reached 29.0 mg/L at a nitrate 
concentration of 200 mg NO3
−-N/L, the COD removal remained above 
80 %. In contrast, reactor R2, which combined microaeration and nitrate 
addition, demonstrated decreased effluent sulfide concentration as ni­
trate addition increased. This reduction can be attributed to sulfide 
oxidation to elemental sulfur or sulfate facilitated by SOB (Nguyen and 
Khanal, 2018). On day 166, when the R2 and R3 operated stably under 
nitrate concentration of 200 mg NO3
−-N/L, the effluent sulfide concen­
tration in R2 was measured at as low as 0.3 mg/L. H2S production 
decreased in both R2 and R3 as the nitrate concentration increased, 
likely due to the nitrate-promoted enrichment of SoNRB, which inhibi­
ted the sulfate reduction process (Cai et al., 2021; Greene et al., 2003). 
Under identical nitrate conditions, R2 exhibited significantly lower H2S 
production than R3, underscoring the enhanced effectiveness of the 
combined microaeration and nitrate approach in reducing sulfide levels. 
Specifically, at a nitrate nitrogen concentration of 200 mg NO3
−-N/L, H2S 
production in R2 was 23.1 mg/d, representing a 95.5 % reduction 
compared to R1 under non-microaerated conditions. This pronounced 
reduction in R2 was likely associated with a higher abundance of SOB 
(Nguyen and Khanal, 2018).
Methane production in the different reactors is shown in Fig. 2(h). 
During the initial 135 days, reactor R1 exhibited stable methane pro­
duction ranging from 0.63 ± 0.052 to 0.65 ± 0.066 L/d. Following the 
introduction of microaeration, methane production increased signifi­
cantly, reaching 1.22 ± 0.055 L/d on day 166, which was 1.88 times 
higher than that in the non-microaerated period. Methane production in 
reactors R2 and R3 exceeded that of control group R1 under non- 
microaerated conditions (day 135) and increased with increasing ni­
trate concentrations. Reactor R2 exhibited higher methane production 
compared to Reactor R3 (0.86 ± 0.077 to 1.21 ± 0.066 L/d) at the same 
nitrate concentration, maintaining methane production values between 
1.40 ± 0.088 and 1.57 ± 0.096 L/d. This was 2.15–2.42 times the 
methane production of R1 under non-microaerated condition (day 135), 
and 1.15 to 1.29 times that of R1 under microaeration alone. These 
findings highlight the synergistic effect of microaeration and nitrate 
addition, which significantly enhanced methane production during the 
anaerobic treatment of SOW. This improvement can be attributed to the 
combined conditions effectively reducing sulfide concentrations in the 
system, thereby alleviating the inhibitory effects of sulfides on microbial 
growth and metabolism and ultimately improving methane production 
(Muller et al., 2022; Ruan et al., 2019). Based on a reactor working 
volume of 4.7 L and a hydraulic retention time of 24 h, the baseline 
methane production was estimated at 134.04–138.30 L per cubic meter 
of wastewater. In contrast, microaeration combined with nitrate addi­
tion (100–200 mg NO3
−-N/L) increased methane yield to 185.65–195.69 
L per cubic meter of wastewater. Using the lower heating value of 
methane (35.88 MJ/m3), this improvement corresponds to an additional 
energy recovery of 6.67–7.02 MJ per cubic meter of wastewater. At a DO 
concentration of 0.20–0.25 mg/L, the electricity consumption associ­
ated with microaeration was approximately 0.4 kWh per cubic meter of

3.2. Sludge characteristics
3.2.1. Particle size distribution
Particle size distributions and morphological observations of the 
sludge are shown in Fig. 3(a) and Fig. S3. Sludge with a particle size 
greater than 0.2 mm is typically classified as granular sludge (Liu et al., 
2020). After 135 days of operation, the proportion of granular sludge in 
R1 was only 5.5 %. However, when the operating conditions were 
changed to microaeration, the proportion increased to 10.2 % within 32 
days. This finding suggests that microaerobic conditions promote sludge 
granulation by reducing sulfide production and creating a more favor­
able environment for microbial growth and metabolic activity. Previous 
studies have shown that microaeration enhances intracellular electron 
transfer and metabolic activity, which leads to increased ATP generation 
and promotes the secretion of EPS (Wu et al., 2024). These EPS act as 
biological adhesives that facilitate particle aggregation and granulation 
(Wu et al., 2024). In reactors R2 and R3, the proportion of granular 
sludge (particles >0.2 mm) was significantly higher, at 55.6 % and 37.7 
%, respectively. The enhanced granulation observed in R2 and R3 can be 
attributed to the suppression of sulfate reduction, which mitigates the 
inhibitory effects of sulfides on microbial growth. Reactor R2, which was 
operated under combined microaerobic conditions and nitrate supple­
mentation, exhibited the highest granulation. This indicated that the 
synergistic effects of microaeration and nitrate addition effectively 
accelerated sludge granulation. It is also noteworthy that the hydraulic 
shear generated by the external aeration recirculation system further 
enhanced sludge granulation by facilitating particle collisions and 
increasing aggregate compactness (Chen et al., 2020).
3.2.2. Settling property and VSS/TSS ratio
The variations in SVI30 and VSS/TSS ratios are shown in Fig. 3(b). 
The SVI30 values in all three reactors decreased progressively, reaching 
<45 mL/g by Day 166. This result indicated that granular sludge with 
excellent settling properties had been developed. Among the reactors, 
R2 exhibited the lowest SVI30, and this is likely because it contained a 
higher proportion of granular sludge. The VSS/TSS ratio followed a 
trend of an initial increase and then a gradual decrease over time. During 
the early operational stages, heightened microbial activity in the sludge 
led to the accumulation of organic matter, such as cytoplasmic material 
and metabolic byproducts, thereby increasing the VSS fraction. How­
ever, as the operational time progressed, the accumulation of inorganic 
solids, including salts, likely contributed to an increase in TSS, resulting 
in a decline in the VSS/TSS ratio (Chen et al., 2019). By day 166, the 
VSS/TSS ratio in reactors R1, R2, and R3 had stabilized at approximately 
0.7, reflecting high metabolic activity in the sludge (Corsino et al., 
2017).
3.2.3. EPS
EPS secreted by microorganisms play a crucial role in sludge gran­
ulation and serve as a key indicators of microbial metabolism. The 
variations in the EPS content across the different reactors are shown in 
Fig. 3(c). Consistent with a previous study (Liang et al., 2019), the EPS 
content initially increased and subsequently decreased during granula­
tion. During the first 112 d, reactor R2 exhibited a consistently higher 
EPS content than R1 and R3, indicating that the combined effects of 
microaeration and nitrate addition created more favorable conditions 
for microbial EPS secretion. This enhancement may be attributed to two 
synergistic mechanisms: (1) microaeration may enhance microbial 
metabolic activity and energy availability, which could promote EPS 
secretion (Wu et al., 2024); and (2) nitrate addition facilitated the 
enrichment of EPS-producing denitrifying bacteria such as Thauera and 
unclassified_f_Rhodocyclaceae, as identified in Section 3.3. These micro­
organisms are known to secrete substantial amounts of EPS to enhance 
biofilm and granule formation under denitrifying conditions. An 
elevated EPS content not only increases microbial adhesion and

3.3.1. Microbial richness and diversity
Microbial communities in sludge samples from different reactors 
were analyzed via high-throughput sequencing, including seeded sludge 
(S0), reactor R1 without microaeration (R1-135), R1 with microaeration 
(R1-166), R2 with microaeration and 100 mg NO3
−-N/L nitrate (R2-112), 
R2 with microaeration and 200 mg NO3

100 mg NO3

−-N/L nitrate 
(R3-166). The diversity indices of the samples are represented in 
Table 1. All samples exhibited coverage exceeding 0.99, indicating that 
the sequencing results accurately reflected microbial community struc­
tures. Higher values of the abundance-based coverage estimator (ACE) 
and Chao indices indicate increased microbial community richness, 
while a higher Shannon index reflects greater microbial diversity. The 
ACE and Chao indices ranked as follows: (R2-112, R2-166) > R1-166 >
(R3-112, R3-166) > R1-135. These results indicate that microaeration 
and nitrate addition enhanced microbial community richness, with the 
highest richness observed under combined microaeration and nitrate 
supplementation conditions. A comparison of the Shannon diversity 
index between R1-135 and R1-166 revealed that microaeration alone 
slightly reduced the microbial diversity. However, the Shannon indices 
for reactors R2 and R3 showed an increasing trend with increasing ni­
trate concentration, with R2 consistently exhibiting higher microbial 
diversity. This increase in microbial diversity is likely linked to reduced 
sulfide concentrations, which mitigate their inhibitory effects on mi­
crobial proliferation in anaerobic systems.
Non-metric multidimensional scaling analysis (Fig. S4) demon­
strated that the S0 sample was clearly separated from the other sludge 
samples, indicating a substantial shift in microbial community structure 
after cultivation in SOW. The shortest distance was observed between 
R1-135 and R1-166, suggesting that microaeration alone exerted a 
relatively limited effect on the microbial community structure compared 
to nitrate addition or the combined effects of microaeration and nitrate. 
The distances between R1-135 and R2-112 or R2-166 were significantly 
greater, indicating that the interaction between microaeration and ni­
trate caused pronounced changes in the microbial community structure 
within the anaerobic reactor. These shifts in the microbial community 
structure are likely the primary factors underlying the observed differ­
ences in organic matter removal efficiency and H2S production among 
the reactors.
3.3.2. Microbial community composition
The microbial community composition at the phylum level is shown 
in Fig. 4(a). The dominant phyla in seed sludge (S0) were Proteobacteria 
(39.4 %), Desulfobacterota (16.1 %), and Chloroflexi (13.8 %). After 
135 d of cultivation with SOW, the dominant phyla in R1 shifted to 
Proteobacteria (21.2 %), Bacteroidota (23.3 %), Firmicutes (22.7 %), 
and Desulfobacterota (12.8 %). When R1 was operated under microa­
eration, the relative abundance of Caldisericota in R1-166 increased to 
21.3 %. In contrast, the relative abundances of Proteobacteria and Fir­
micutes decreased by 15.9 % and 12.8 %, respectively. Sludge samples 
from R2 (R2-112 and R2-166) and R3 (R3-112 and R3-166) demon­
strated higher relative abundances of Chloroflexi, Actinobacteriota, and 
Hydrogenedentes than those from R1-135. The abundance of these 
phyla was positively correlated with increasing nitrate concentrations. 
Previous studies have shown that Chloroflexi and Actinobacteriota 
contribute to enhanced methane production (de Sousa e Silva et al., 
2024). Members of the Chloroflexi family play critical roles in organic 
matter hydrolysis and nitrogen cycling (Zhang et al., 2021). Moreover, 
some SOB within Chloroflexi can oxidize sulfur to sulfate (Luo et al., 
2020). Actinobacteriota can efficiently remove contaminants from 
highly concentrated organic wastewater (Zhong et al., 2023), whereas 
Hydrogenedentes can hydrolyze organic pollutants into acetate (Nobu 
et al., 2015). The increased abundance of these phyla likely contributed 
to enhanced organic matter degradation in the nitrate-supplemented 
reactors. At the same nitrate concentration, reactor R2 exhibited a 
significantly higher abundance of organic matter-degrading bacteria 
such as Chloroflexi, Hydrogenedentes, Synergistota, and Armatimona­

Furthermore, R2-166 showed a greater abundance of Euryarchaeota and

elevated abundance of methane-producing archaea enhanced the 
methane production in R2 under the synergistic effects of nitrate addi­

microaerobic environment facilitated the proliferation of facultatively 
anaerobic bacteria, as reflected by a 4.86 % reduction in anaerobic

0.05 %. Facultative fermenters, with their rapid oxygen consumption 
capacity, are likely to deplete dissolved oxygen, thereby creating pro­

were more abundant in R2 and R3 at a nitrate concentration of 100 mg 
NO3

increased to 200 mg NO3
−-N/L, the relative abundance of these bacteria 
decreased. The dynamics of biofilm-forming microbes correspond to 
changes in the EPS content during sludge granulation. Moreover, the 
reduced abundance of stress-tolerant microbes at 200 mg NO3

PICRUSt2 was employed to predict functional genes potentially 
involved in sulfate reduction, sulfur oxidation, and methanogenesis. The 
results are shown in Fig. 4(d–f). The sulfate-reducing metabolism in­

fate reduction (DSR). The first step in both pathways is the conversion of 
sulfate to adenosine-5′-phosphosulfate (APS), mediated by the key gene 
sat. Compared to R1-135, sat was downregulated in both R2 and R3, 
indicating that nitrate addition, either alone or in combination with 
microaeration, significantly inhibited the conversion of sulfate to APS 
(Cai et al., 2021). This trend corresponds to a marked reduction in the 
SRA under these conditions. Genes involved in the ASR, including cysC, 
cysJ, and cysI, were downregulated in sludge samples from reactors R2 
and R3, with the most pronounced decrease observed in R2-166. In the 
DSR metabolic pathway, dsrA and dsrB showed a decline in R1-166, 
whereas sat, aprA, and aprB were upregulated. However, the 
DSR-related genes (sat, aprA, aprB, dsrA, and dsrB) were significantly

inhibit sulfate reduction through different mechanisms. Specifically, in

over SRB for substrates (Xu et al., 2017). In contrast, under the com­
bined nitrate and microaeration conditions, DSR-related genes in R2 
showed a slight increase as nitrate concentrations increased. This could 
be attributed to the enhanced pollutant conversion, generating more 
organic acids, which may mitigate substrate competition between NRB 
and SRB, thereby slightly promoting the SRB profile. This phenomenon 
can be attributed to the enhanced conversion of pollutants, generating 
more organic acids. These organic acids may alleviate substrate 
competition between NRB and SRB, thereby modestly favoring SRB 
activity. Compared with the control (R1-135), genes associated with 
sulfur oxidation were upregulated under microaeration, nitrate addi­
tion, and their combination (Fig. 4(e)), suggesting an enrichment of SOB 
in the anaerobic digestion system. Furthermore, the sulfur oxidation 
genes SoxX, SoxY, SoxZ, SoxB, SoxC, and SorA exhibited higher abun­
dance under the synergistic effects of nitrate and microaeration. This 
may account for the lower sulfide concentrations and reduced hydrogen 
sulfide production observed in R2. Key genes involved in methano­
genesis, such as mtrA, hdrD, and mer, which mediate acetate fermenta­

microaeration and nitrate addition effectively enhanced methane 
metabolic activity, consistent with the elevated methane production 
observed in reactor R2. It should be emphasized that the PICRUSt2 
analysis provides predicted functional potentials rather than direct 
measurements of gene expression, representing possible rather than 
actual metabolic activities of microbial communities. Therefore, these 
predictive results should be interpreted with caution and regarded as 
preliminary indications that require further validation through meta­
genomic or metatranscriptomic sequencing.
3.4. Mechanisms of microaeration and nitrate synergy in enhancing SOW 
treatment
The synergistic mechanisms through which nitrate and microaerobic 
conditions enhance the anaerobic digestion of SOW were elucidated 
based on the sludge characteristics and microbial community composi­
tion (Fig. 5). External circulation aeration facilitated the volatilization of 
a small portion of H2S. Based on a static gas-liquid equilibrium 
assumption, the concentrations of dissolved H2S in reactors R1, R2, and 
R3 on day 166 were calculated to be 0.24, 0.01, and 3.98 mg/L, 
respectively, by accounting for total sulfide concentration, system pH, 
and the dissociation equilibrium of H2S. Accordingly, H2S volatilization 
associated with aeration was estimated to account for only approxi­
mately 0.19 %, 0.0077 %, and 3.08 % of the total influent sulfur per day 
in R1, R2, and R3, respectively. These findings suggest that H2S vola­
tilization was minimal and can be considered negligible in the overall 
sulfur balance. Conversely, the introduction of microaeration-enriched 
fermentative bacteria, such as Lentimicrobium, Longilinea, nor­
ank_f_Cloacimonadaceae, and Blvii28_wastewater-sludge_group, enhanced 
the hydrolysis and fermentation of organic matter into VFAs (Hu et al., 
2022a; Huang et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2017). Moreover, 
the combined effects of nitrate and microaeration promoted the prolif­
eration of SOB, including Sulfurospirillum and Thauera, leading to sig­
nificant upregulation of sulfur oxidation-related genes such as SoxB,

3.5. Proposal of a practical application strategy
This study demonstrated that, compared to the control reactor, 
which was operated without microaeration or nitrate addition, main­
taining a DO concentration of 0.20–0.25 mg/L and adding 100–200 mg 
NO3
−-N/L of nitrate led to a reduction in H2S production by 79.2–95.5 % 
while improving COD removal efficiency by 49.1–50.8 % and methane 
production by 138.5–141.5 %. These observations were derived from 
laboratory-scale experiments using glucose as the primary carbon 
source, which was deliberately selected to facilitate mechanistic inves­
tigation under well-controlled conditions. Based on these findings, a 
potential strategy is proposed for the treatment of LCDA wastewater 
from petrochemical enterprises (Fig. 6). In this conceptual process, 
maintaining a DO concentration of 0.20–0.25 mg/L, together with the 
addition of 100–200 NO3
−-N mg/L nitrate, is expected to significantly 
reduce H2S production, enhance COD removal efficiency, and increase 
methane production, as demonstrated in our laboratory-scale experi­
ments. The nitrate nitrogen required for this process could be sourced 
from refinery flue gas denitrification wastewater.
LCDA wastewater, generated from the microbial fermentation of n- 
alkanes (C10–C18), is mainly composed of sulfate, dicarboxylates, and 
fermentation medium components, among which glucose constitutes the 
dominant biodegradable carbon substrate. It is characterized by a low 
pH (3.0–4.5) and a high concentration of COD (>6000 mg/L), sulfate

Drawing on previous studies (Chen et al., 2023a), we suggest that pre­
treatment with 15 g/L CaCl2 and 20 g/L polyaluminum chloride (PAC) 
could effectively remove total phosphorus and sulfate through precipi­
tation and coagulation processes. Specifically, calcium ions react with 
phosphate ions to form Ca3(PO4)2 and Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2, while PAC 
hydrolysis products (Ala) and sulfate ions co-precipitate as Ca4A­
l6O12SO4. The resulting solid precipitates could be repurposed as raw 
materials for calcium sulfoaluminate cement production, supporting 
resource recovery. In addition, small organic molecules such as organic 
acids, alcohols, and amines can be removed through adsorption, coag­
ulation, and co-precipitation, significantly reducing COD and other 
pollutants. Following pretreatment, the LCDA wastewater would be 
mixed with nitrate-rich refinery flue gas denitrification wastewater at a 
1:1 volumetric ratio, and the mixture would be introduced into a UASB 
reactor equipped with an external aeration device. Maintaining a 
recirculation ratio of 200 % and a DO level of 0.20–0.25 mg/L is 
anticipated to optimize the biological processes, based on the opera­
tional conditions that yielded stable performance and synergistic sulfur 
control in the present study. The gases released during aeration could be 
scrubbed with NaOH prior to discharge, and the methane generated 
could be purified and utilized for energy recovery within the refinery. 
The final effluent is expected to meet the influent quality standards of 
petroleum wastewater treatment plants. This integrated treatment 
strategy is designed to enable the co-management of LCDA and 
nitrate-rich refinery wastewater, supporting circular resource utilization 
by reusing waste-derived nitrate and advancing sustainable wastewater 
management through “waste-to-treat-waste” approach. It should be 
emphasized that this strategy represents a proposed conceptual design, 
intended to illustrate the potential application of our research findings. 
To date, no pilot- or full-scale experiments have been conducted to 
validate this process. Further research using real LCDA wastewater is 
therefore required to assess the long-term stability, robustness, and en­
gineering feasibility of the proposed strategy under practical operating 
conditions.
4. Conclusions
In this study, we systematically investigated the influence of 
different nitrate concentrations under microaerobic conditions on 
enhancing anaerobic digestion in SOW. The combined application of 
nitrate (100–200 mg NO3
−-N/L) and microaeration (DO: 0.20–0.25 mg/ 
L) synergistically promoted EPS secretion and granular sludge forma­
tion. This operational strategy effectively inhibited the proliferation of 
SRB (Desulfovibrio) while selectively enriching SOB (e.g., Sulfurospirillum 
and Thauera) and methanogens (e.g., Methanosaeta and Meth­
anobacterium). Sulfate reduction genes (aprA, aprB, dsrA, and dsrB) were 
downregulated, whereas sulfur oxidation genes (SoxX, SoxY, SoxZ, 
SoxB, SoxC, and SorA) and methanogenesis-related genes (mtrA, hdrD, 
and mer) were upregulated. The suppression of sulfide production alle­
viated its inhibitory effects on anaerobic digestion, significantly 
improving COD removal efficiency (48.2–49.8 %) and methane pro­
duction (138.5–141.5 %). These findings provide mechanistic insights 
into the interactions between microaeration and nitrate addition, of­
fering a promising strategy for optimizing the anaerobic treatment of 
SOW and controlling sulfide production. However, future work should 
aim to validate these results using multi-omics and real-world applica­
tions to further refine the practical viability of this approach.
